journey.title: What is Islam?

verse.text: We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: there is no god worthy of worship except Me, so worship Me.

videos.blurb: One God. One message. Peace through surrender.
notes: “Islam” comes from the root s-l-m — the same root as salām, peace: peace found by willingly surrendering to the One who made you.
A “Muslim” is simply anyone who submits to God alone — it describes a relationship, not an ethnicity.
No priesthood stands in between: the surrender is offered to God directly.

videos.blurb: The same call carried by Abraham, Moses and Jesus.
notes: Islam presents itself as the original faith of every prophet — Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus — renewed, not invented.
What Muhammad ﷺ brought is the final edition of one continuous message: worship the One God alone.
That is why entering Islam is often called reverting — a return, not a conversion.

journey.summary: Islam simply means peace through submission to the One God. Muslims believe the same God who spoke to Abraham, Moses and Jesus sent a final, complete message to all of humanity.
points: “Islam” shares its root with the word for peace, salām.
One God, no intermediaries — a direct relationship.
The same core message carried by every prophet before.

journey.title: Why are we here?

verse.text: Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would never be returned to Us?

videos.blurb: Why is there anything at all — and why are you here?
notes: Before comparing religions, an honest mind asks the first question: why does anything exist at all?
Whatever begins needs a cause beyond itself — nothing brings itself into being.
Shrugging the question off isn’t neutrality; it’s an unexamined answer.

videos.blurb: Design points to a Designer — and you to a purpose.
notes: Order, fine-tuning and law-like nature read like intention, not accident.
If you were made on purpose, your life has a purpose — and the Maker is the One who defines it.
The Qur’an asks it directly: did you think We created you without purpose? (23:115)

journey.summary: Before any religion is named, there is a question every heart carries: what is all this for? Everything designed points to a designer — and purpose only makes sense if we were made on purpose.
points: Your innate sense already reaches for something greater.
This question deserves an honest answer, not a shrug.

journey.title: Who is God?

verse.text: There is nothing like Him — and He alone is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.

videos.blurb: Tawḥīd — the purest idea of God.
notes: Tawḥīd: God is One — no partners, no rivals, no family, no equals.
Every act of worship — prayer, deepest hope, deepest fear, ultimate gratitude — belongs to Him alone.
This is the dividing line between Islam and every form of idolatry, ancient or modern.

videos.blurb: Creator, not creation — near, without needing.
notes: God is the Creator, not part of creation — nothing He made resembles Him (42:11).
He needs nothing — no rest, no food, no help — while everything needs Him.
Yet He is near: He hears every prayer directly, with no intermediary required.

journey.summary: In Islam, God (Allah) is One — with no partner, no image, and nothing like Him. He is the Creator, not a part of creation; near enough to hear you, without ever needing you.
points: You can call on Him directly, any time, in any language.

journey.title: Is the Qur’an from God?

verse.text: If you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a chapter like it…

videos.blurb: The claim the Qur’an makes about itself.
notes: The Qur’an claims to be God’s literal speech — not a book about God, but a message from Him.
Revealed over 23 years to a man who could not read or write — yet it reshaped language, law and history.
Its constant method: look, think, reason — and then submit.
One text, letter for letter, from Indonesia to Morocco — memorised whole by millions in every generation.
Manuscripts across fourteen centuries match — the preservation is testable, not a slogan.
The Qur’an promised this itself: “It is We who sent down the Reminder, and We will surely guard it.” (15:9)

videos.blurb: Produce one chapter like it — still unanswered.
notes: The Qur’an dares its doubters: produce a single chapter like it (2:23).
Arabia’s master poets — with every motive to win — never met the challenge; fourteen centuries on, it still stands.
A standing, testable challenge is simply not how human books speak.

journey.summary: The Qur’an claims to be God’s own words, revealed to Muhammad ﷺ and preserved unchanged for over 1,400 years. Its language and insight are, Muslims hold, beyond what any person could author.
points: An open challenge no one has met: produce anything like it.
Not only what to believe — but how, and why, to live.

journey.title: Who is Muhammad ﷺ?

verse.text: We have sent you only as a mercy for the whole world.

videos.blurb: Known for truth before he ever preached.
notes: Before revelation, Makkah already called him al-Amīn — the Trustworthy; even his opponents deposited valuables with him.
He was offered wealth and kingship to stop preaching; he refused it all and lived simply until his death.
Liars profit from their lies — his life shows a man who only lost worldly comfort by speaking.

videos.blurb: How he lived — and why it matters to you.
notes: Sent “as a mercy to the worlds” (21:107) — his teaching protected women, orphans, the poor, even animals.
His final sermon: no Arab above a non-Arab, no white above black — standing is by piety alone.
To follow him is to imitate mercy: gentleness at home, honesty in trade, dignity for the weakest.

journey.summary: Muhammad ﷺ was called “the trustworthy” long before he preached. He asked for no wealth and no power — only that people worship the One God. In his life and character, Muslims see the mark of a true messenger.
points: Trusted for his honesty before prophethood ever began.
Sought no crown and no riches — only to convey the message.
The last in a long line of prophets, sent for everyone.

journey.title: What happens now?

verse.text: Say: O My servants who have wronged themselves — do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.

journey.summary: If your heart accepts that God is One and Muhammad ﷺ is His messenger, entering Islam is simple — a single, sincere sentence. No fee. No ceremony required. Then, gently, at your own pace.
points: Belief first, then a sincere declaration — the Shahada.
Begin with prayer; grow one step at a time.
You are never alone — help is one tap away.

questions.q: What do Muslims believe about Jesus?
questions.html:
Muslims love Jesus (ʿĪsā, peace be upon him) deeply. He is one of the greatest messengers of God — born miraculously of the Virgin Mary, who has an entire chapter of the Qur’an named after her. He healed and gave life by God’s permission, and Muslims believe God raised him up and that he will return.

The one difference: Muslims honour Jesus as the Messiah and a mighty messenger, but worship God alone — just as, Muslims believe, Jesus himself did. No one can be a Muslim without believing in him.

questions.q: If God is good, why is there suffering?
questions.html:
Islam answers this without pretending pain isn’t real. This life is a test, not the destination — a brief chapter before an eternal one. Suffering can purify, awaken, and raise a person’s rank with God, and nothing endured is lost with Him.

Perfect justice is coming: every wrong will be accounted for and every innocent pain compensated on the Day of Judgement. And meanwhile, Muslims aren’t told to accept suffering passively — relieving it is itself worship.

questions.html:
Fourteen centuries ago, Islam gave women the right to own property, inherit, consent to marriage, keep their own name, and seek knowledge — rights many societies granted only recently. The Qur’an addresses women and men as spiritual equals before God.

The hijab is an act of devotion a woman offers to God — and the Qur’an commands men to modesty first, before it addresses women. Where Muslim cultures fall short of this, that is culture failing Islam’s standard — a distinction Muslims themselves insist on.

questions.html:
The Qur’an teaches that taking one innocent life is like killing all of humanity — and saving one is like saving all of humanity (5:32). Islam’s rules of conduct, written 1,400 years ago, forbid harming women, children and non-combatants.

Terrorism violates these teachings, and its victims worldwide are most often Muslims themselves. Almost two billion Muslims live today as ordinary, peaceful neighbours; a faith is judged by its teachings and the norm of its people, not by those who betray both.

questions.html: Allah is simply the Arabic word for God — the One God of Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews say “Allah” in their own prayers and Bibles. Muslims aren’t calling to a new god, but back to the same One.

questions.q: What about people who never heard of Islam?
questions.html: God is perfectly just — more just than any of us. The Qur’an states that God does not punish a people until a messenger’s message has reached them (17:15). People are accountable only for what genuinely reached them, and God — who knows every heart and every circumstance — will judge each soul with complete fairness. No one slips through the cracks of His justice or His mercy.

questions.q: Will I have to change my name, my family, my whole life?
questions.html:
No. You keep your name (unless it carries a meaning against faith), your family, and your love for them. In fact, the Qur’an places kindness to parents — including non-Muslim parents — right next to the worship of God.

Islam entered the world gradually over 23 years, and you’re allowed the same gentleness: begin with belief and prayer, and grow step by step.

questions.html:
The Qur’an’s repeated command is to look — at the sky, the embryo, the honeybee, the alternation of night and day — and to reason. That spirit built a civilisation of science: algebra carries an Arabic name, and Muslim scholars led optics, medicine and astronomy for centuries.

In Islam, studying creation is a way of knowing the Creator; faith and reason are companions, not rivals — which is why this journey began with an argument, not a demand.

questions.q: Do I need to learn Arabic?
questions.html: You can speak to God in any language, at any moment — He hears you. The five daily prayers use a few short Arabic phrases that new Muslims learn gradually, with easy allowances while you’re learning. Millions of Muslims aren’t Arabs; Arabic unites the worship, but it has never been the ticket in.

questions.q: I’ve done terrible things. Would God even accept me?
questions.html:
Yes — and more than accept you. When a person embraces Islam, everything before it is erased completely. A man once came to the Prophet ﷺ afraid his past would follow him in, and was told: Islam demolishes whatever came before it. You don’t carry the old record across; you begin again, clean.

And God goes further still: for those who turn to Him sincerely, He promises not just to erase bad deeds but to replace them with good ones (Qur’an 25:70). His widest invitation is addressed exactly to the person who feels furthest away: “O My servants who have transgressed against themselves — do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins” (39:53). No one is too far gone. The only door He asks you never to walk through is despair.

questions.html: Then take your time — sincerely. The Qur’an itself says there is no compulsion in religion (2:256). A shahada should come from conviction, not pressure, and the door does not close. Keep reading, keep asking — and a real person is one tap away whenever a question is sitting on your chest.

days.html: You are now Muslim, and your slate is wiped completely clean — the Prophet ﷺ taught that embracing Islam erases everything that came before it. Whatever you’re feeling — tears, lightness, even nervousness — is normal, and beautiful.

days.title: Talk to God — in your own words
days.html: Duʿā (supplication) needs no ritual, no Arabic and no set time. Speak to Him in your own language, about anything, as often as you like. This relationship is direct — and it’s yours now.
days.text: Duʿā (supplication) needs no ritual, no Arabic and no set time. Speak to Him in your own language, about anything, as often as you like. This relationship is direct — and it’s yours now.

days.title: Meet the prayer, gently
days.html: Muslims pray five short prayers a day. Don’t panic: begin by standing beside someone and following along — the masjid will happily teach you, and there are easy allowances while you learn the words.
days.text: Muslims pray five short prayers a day. Don’t panic: begin by standing beside someone and following along — the masjid will happily teach you, and there are easy allowances while you learn the words.

days.title: Learn wudu — the two-minute wash
days.html: Before praying, Muslims wash the hands, face, arms and feet — a simple, refreshing ritual called wudu. Anyone at the masjid can show you in minutes; it becomes second nature within a week.

days.title: Tell someone — when it’s safe to
days.html: Community carries you: a Muslim friend, the Ask-a-Muslim line, your local masjid. And if your family situation is delicate, know this — your Islam is fully valid in private. God sees you; there is no deadline for announcing.

days.title: Don’t sprint
days.html: Revelation came down over 23 years — you’re not meant to absorb everything in a weekend. Scholars advise new Muslims to build gradually; at the start, the prayer is the priority. One step, then the next.

days.title: Stay connected
days.html: Read one verse a day in the Qur’an tab — one is enough. Join a new-Muslim class at a masjid near you, and iERA’s new-Muslim programme offers step-by-step courses with a community of people exactly where you are.
